title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol cont: John 15:16 — we did not choose; do not confuse destined and temporal adoption
latin: Sol. (cont.) Augustinus fere hoc caput primum ad Ephesios explicando percurrit. Apponam solummodo haec paucula. Electionem quam significavit Dominus dicens, Non vos me elegistis, sed ego vos elegi; nec fides ipsa praecedit. Non enim quia credidimus, sed ut credamus elegit nos, ne priores eum elegisse dicamur. Periculoso igitur errore confundunt destinatam adoptionem in aeterno actu electionis Divinae cum perfecta adoptione in temporali effectu vocationis efficacis.
pass_a: Solution (continued). Augustine nearly runs through this first chapter to the Ephesians in explaining. I will add only these few things. The election which the Lord signified saying, You did not choose me, but I chose you; nor does faith itself precede. For not because we believed, but that we may believe he chose us, lest we be said to have chosen him first. By a dangerous error therefore they confuse destined adoption in the eternal act of the Divine election with perfect adoption in the temporal effect of efficacious vocation.
pass_b: Sol. (cont.) Augustine nearly walks this first chapter of Ephesians in explaining it. Only a few notes: the election the Lord meant by You did not choose me, but I chose you — and faith itself does not come first. He chose us not because we believed, but that we may believe, lest we be said to have chosen him first. So they dangerously confuse destined adoption in the eternal act of divine election with finished adoption in the temporal effect of efficacious vocation.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol cont: faith may accompany temporal adoption — not eternal destinatio; chain from election
latin: Praecedat fides, aut comitetur saltem adoptionem in ipsis electis peractam: at non potest (vel secundum nostrum considerandi modum) praecedere adoptionem in mente Dei eligentis ab aeterno certis personis decretam et destinatam. Nam fidem salutiferam praecedit vocatio efficax, vel secundum propositum; talem vocationem antecedit praedestinatio sive electio ad gloriam: unde clarum est, non considerari ullos aut praevideri tanquam fideles nisi ex antecedente praedestinationis decreto, quia efficax vocatio, vera fides, et realis adoptio inde dimanat.
pass_a: Let faith precede, or at least accompany, adoption perfected in the elect themselves: but it cannot (even according to our mode of considering) precede the adoption decreed and destined in the mind of God electing from eternity for certain persons. For efficacious vocation, or according to purpose, precedes saving faith; predestination or election to glory precedes such vocation: whence it is clear that none are considered or foreseen as faithful except from the antecedent decree of predestination, because efficacious vocation, true faith, and real adoption flow thence.
pass_b: Faith may precede or at least go with adoption finished in the elect themselves — but it cannot (even on our way of thinking) precede the adoption God from eternity decreed and destined for certain persons in his electing mind. Efficacious vocation according to purpose precedes saving faith; predestination or election to glory precedes that vocation. So none are considered or foreseen as faithful except from the antecedent predestination decree — because efficacious vocation, true faith, and real adoption flow from it.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol cont: benevolence toward elect still in sin — Orange 25; Scotus; two acceptations
latin: Porro, quod dicunt, Deum neminem in Christo gratum facere aut habere nisi fidelem, id nullo modo potest consistere. Quaero enim, Unde nascitur efficax propositum in Deo, inspirandi fidem salutiferam et poenitentiam cordibus humanis? In hoc ipso proposito quod spectat adhuc infideles et impoenitentes, singularem ac specialem quendam Dei amorem agnoscant est necesse. Tantus enim est Dei amor erga Filium suum unigenitum, ut ejus intuitu amore aeternae benevolentiae complectatur eos omnes, quos in illo elegit, etiam in statu peccati et infidelitatis consideratos; et propterea speciali quadam gratia curat semper eos ex hoc statu eruendos. Praeclare in hanc sententiam Concilium Arausicanum, Displicentes amati sumus, ut fieret in nobis unde placeremus, can. 25. Hisce adde, Christum esse caput tam infinitae potentiae, ejusque meritum tantae efficaciae, ut influere possit in membra nondum unita, sed solummodo destinata, et suo influxu efficere ut talia uniantur. Hoc illud est quod Scotus bene observavit, lib. 3. dist. 19. Christus meruit ut non conjuncta sibi conjungerentur: et in hoc potissimum consistit meritum ejus. Si Christi meritum ad non-conjunctos, hoc est, non-credentes, pertingit, efficitque ut conjungantur, tum etiam et conformis quaedam Dei acceptatio sive gratificatio ad eosdem extenditur. Brevius itaque respondeo, Hominem aliquem dici posse Deo acceptum in Christo, vel propter Christum, dupliciter. Uno modo, quando illum complectitur amore quasi praesentis amicitiae, illumque ut domesticum ad thronum gratiae admittit, atque sensu favoris sui beat. Hoc sensu soli fideles sunt in Christo Deo grati. Alio modo intelligi potest aliquis esse prae aliis Deo gratus et acceptus, nimirum, quando illum complectitur amore aeternae benevolentiae, ut praedestinatum Filii sui membrum. Licet enim adhuc paterni amoris effecta ad talem non defundantur, intendit tamen in Christo et propter Christum idoneo tempore diffundere. Et hoc sensu Deus multos etiam nondum credentes et conversos gratos sibi fecit in Christo, non tanquam jam positos in Christo, sed tanquam ex speciali favore ponendos, quia ab aeterno in Christo electos.
pass_a: Further, what they say, That God makes or holds no one pleasing in Christ except a faithful one, can in no way stand. For I ask, Whence is born the efficacious purpose in God of inspiring saving faith and repentance into human hearts? In this very purpose which still regards unbelievers and the impenitent, it is necessary that they acknowledge a certain singular and special love of God. For so great is God's love toward his only-begotten Son, that in view of him with the love of eternal benevolence he embraces all those whom he elected in him, even considered in the state of sin and unbelief; and therefore by a certain special grace he always cares that they be drawn out of this state. Most clearly to this sentence the Council of Orange, Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please, can. 25. To these add, that Christ is a head of such infinite power, and his merit of such efficacy, that he can influence into members not yet united, but only destined, and by his influence bring it about that such be united. This is that which Scotus well observed, book 3 distinction 19. Christ merited that things not joined to him should be joined: and in this chiefly consists his merit. If Christ's merit reaches to the non-joined, that is, non-believers, and brings it about that they be joined, then also a certain conforming acceptance or gratifying of God is extended to the same. More briefly therefore I answer, That a man can be said to be acceptable to God in Christ, or for Christ's sake, in two ways. In one way, when he embraces him with a love as of present friendship, and admits him as a household member to the throne of grace, and blesses him with the sense of his favor. In this sense only the faithful are pleasing to God in Christ. In another way someone can be understood to be pleasing and acceptable to God before others, namely, when he embraces him with the love of eternal benevolence, as a predestinated member of his Son. For although the effects of paternal love are not yet poured out upon such a one, he nonetheless intends in Christ and for Christ's sake to pour them out at a fit time. And in this sense God has made many even not yet believing and converted pleasing to himself in Christ, not as already placed in Christ, but as to be placed by special favor, because elected in Christ from eternity.
pass_b: Further: their claim that God makes or holds none pleasing in Christ except the faithful cannot stand. Whence comes God's efficacious purpose to inspire saving faith and repentance into human hearts? That purpose still regards unbelievers and the impenitent — so they must grant a singular, special love of God there. So great is his love for his only-begotten Son that, looking to him in eternal benevolence, he embraces all he elected in him even while considered in sin and unbelief — and by special grace always works to draw them out of that state. So Orange can. 25: Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. Add: Christ is a head of infinite power, his merit of such efficacy that it can influence members not yet united but only destined, and by that influence unite them. Scotus (3 dist. 19) well noted: Christ merited that the not-yet-joined be joined — and therein his merit chiefly consists. If his merit reaches non-believers and joins them, a conforming divine acceptance extends to them too. Briefly: one may be acceptable to God in Christ, or for Christ's sake, two ways. One: present friendship-love, admitted as a household member to the throne of grace — in that sense only the faithful are pleasing in Christ. Two: eternal benevolence as a predestinated member of his Son — though paternal effects are not yet poured out, he intends in Christ and for Christ to pour them at the fit time. In that sense God has made many not yet believing or converted pleasing in Christ — not as already placed in him, but as to be placed by special favor, because elected in Christ from eternity.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 5 Sol close: Minor — faith a destined means, not a foreseen condition of election
latin: De Minore, quae expressis Scripturae verbis continetur, non opus est aliquid dicam: ex dictis enim facile intelligatur, inde non posse probari, fidem in electione debere considerari ut conditionem praevisam, et electionis antecedaneam, sed ut medium illis destinatum et conferendum quos Deus elegit, et adoptandos destinavit.
pass_a: Concerning the Minor, which is contained in express words of Scripture, there is no need that I say anything: for from what has been said it may easily be understood that thence it cannot be proved that faith in election ought to be considered as a foreseen condition, and antecedent of election, but as a means destined and to be conferred on those whom God elected, and destined to be adopted.
pass_b: On the Minor, which sits in express Scripture words, little need be added: from what is said it is plain you cannot prove from it that faith in election must be taken as a foreseen condition antecedent to election — but as a means destined and to be given to those God elected and destined for adoption.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 6: perpetual use of Electi — in salvation contexts always means believers
latin: Arg. 6. Petitur aliud argumentum a perpetuo usu vocis, Electi, quotiescunque ponitur cum respectu ad salutem; ut Rom. viii. Quis accusabit adversus electos Dei? et Rom. xi. Electi assecuti sunt, et Matth. xxii. Multi vocati, pauci electi. Ex hisce aliisque locis consimilibus ita argumentantur; Vox Electorum, cum de salute agitur, perpetuo in Scripturis usurpatur pro credentibus: Ergo nulla est electio ad salutem nisi credentium.
pass_a: Argument 6. Another argument is sought from the perpetual use of the word Elect, as often as it is placed with respect to salvation; as Rom. 8. Who will accuse against God's elect? and Rom. 11. The elect have obtained, and Matt. 22. Many called, few elect. From these and other like places they argue thus; The word of the Elect, when it is treated concerning salvation, is perpetually used in the Scriptures for believers: Therefore there is no election to salvation except of believers.
pass_b: Arg. 6. Another argument from the standing use of Elect wherever salvation is in view — Rom. 8: Who will accuse God's elect?; Rom. 11: The elect have obtained; Matt. 22: Many called, few elect. From these and like places: the word Elect, when Scripture speaks of salvation, is always used for believers; therefore there is no election to salvation except of believers.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 6 Sol: elect known a posteriori — many elect while still unbelieving; Rom. 8:28–30
latin: Sol. Quando sacrae Scripturae loquuntur de aliquibus designatis personis tanquam de Electis, hoc vocabulum accommodant ad solos credentes: quia nos de arcano Electionis nihil certi habemus nisi a posteriore, hoc est, ab effectis fidei et sanctificationis. Hinc Apostolus credentes Electorum nomine passim solet notare. Verum inde non efficitur, vel debere confundi electos et credentes, vel electionem ex praevisa fide tanquam conditione antecedanea esse suspendendam. Quamvis enim nos non possumus eos electos vocare, quos videmus incredulos, tamen certum est, multos impoenitentes ac incredulos esse tamen interim electos: quod in Paulo, adeoque in omnibus electis, ante efficacem conversionem, verissimum est. Quin etiam cum Praedestinationis et Electionis vocabula in tota hac disputatione promiscue usurpentur, planum est vocem Praedestinatorum, cum de salute agitur, etiam de incredulis usurpari. Nam cum Apostolus Rom. viii. 28. dicit, Quos Praedestinavit, Vocavit; quos vocavit justificavit, &c. aperte ponit Praedestinatos quosdam antecedenter ad vocationem, fidem et justificationem.
pass_a: Solution. When the sacred Scriptures speak of certain designated persons as of the Elect, they accommodate this word to believers alone: because we have nothing certain concerning the secret of Election except from the posterior, that is, from the effects of faith and sanctification. Hence the Apostle is accustomed everywhere to mark believers with the name of the Elect. But thence it is not brought about either that the elect and believers ought to be confused, or that election ought to be suspended from foresight of faith as an antecedent condition. For although we cannot call those elect whom we see unbelieving, yet it is certain that many impenitent and unbelieving are nonetheless meanwhile elect: which in Paul, and so in all the elect, before efficacious conversion, is most true. Moreover since the words of Predestination and Election are used promiscuously in this whole disputation, it is plain that the word of the Predestinated, when it is treated concerning salvation, is used even of unbelievers. For when the Apostle at Rom. 8:28 says, Whom he Predestinated, he Called; whom he called he justified, etc., he openly places certain Predestinated antecedently to vocation, faith, and justification.
pass_b: Sol. When Scripture names designated persons Elect, it fits the word to believers alone — because we know nothing sure of election's secret except a posteriori, from the effects of faith and sanctification. So the Apostle often marks believers as Elect. That does not mean elect and believers must be confused, or that election hangs on foresight of faith as an antecedent condition. We cannot call unbelievers elect as we see them — yet many impenitent and unbelieving are elect in the meantime; true of Paul and of all the elect before efficacious conversion. And since Predestination and Election are used interchangeably in this dispute, Predestinated in salvation-talk is used even of unbelievers. Rom. 8:28ff.: Whom he predestinated, he called; whom he called, he justified — openly sets some Predestinated before vocation, faith, and justification.

lemmas.gloss: known a posteriori from faith's effects

title: Cap. IV Arg. 6 Sol close: actual faith not foresight-faith; invert — nexus not Remonstrant order
latin: Hisce accedat, In illis omnibus locis ubi Electorum nomen tribuitur fidelibus, fidem actualem semper denotari, non illam ante jacta mundi fundamenta in sola Dei praescientia consideratam, quam urgent Remonstrantes. Non recte igitur inferunt; Electus et credens sunt subjecta eadem secundum phrasin Scripturarum: Ergo Electio fit ex praevisa fide; sed, Ergo omnibus electis suo tempore datur fides salutifera. Possem facile hoc argumentum invertere, et contra adversarios sic retorquere, si quid roboris in se haberet, Vox Credentium, cum de credentibus ad salutem agitur, perpetuo intelligitur de electis: Ergo nulla est fides ad salutem nisi electorum; Ergo fides oritur ex antecedente electione. Sed ex tali usu vocabulorum nihil aliud concludi debet, quam fidem et electionem habere inter se quendam nexum: sed utrum ita connectantur ut fides praevisa antecedat electionem tanquam conditio in eligendo praerequisita, (quod volunt Remonstrantes) an ut fides subsequatur electionem tanquam dispositio in omnibus electis debito tempore producenda, ex locis Scripturae allatis non constat. Ea igitur sigillatim expendere minime necessarium est.
pass_a: To these let it be added, That in all those places where the name of the Elect is attributed to the faithful, actual faith is always denoted, not that considered before the foundations of the world were laid in God's foresight alone, which the Remonstrants urge. They therefore do not rightly infer; Elect and believer are the same subjects according to the phrasing of the Scriptures: Therefore Election is made from foresight of faith; but, Therefore to all the elect in their time saving faith is given. I could easily invert this argument, and so twist it back against the adversaries, if it had any strength in itself, The word of Believers, when it is treated concerning believers unto salvation, is perpetually understood of the elect: Therefore there is no faith unto salvation except of the elect; Therefore faith arises from antecedent election. But from such use of vocabularies nothing else ought to be concluded than that faith and election have a certain nexus between them: but whether they are so connected that foresight of faith precedes election as a condition prerequired in electing, (which the Remonstrants will) or that faith follows election as a disposition to be produced in all the elect at the due time, does not stand from the places of Scripture brought. Therefore to weigh those one by one is least necessary.
pass_b: Add: wherever Elect is given to the faithful, actual faith is meant — not faith merely in God's foresight before the world's foundations, which the Remonstrants urge. So they wrongly infer: Elect and believer are the same subjects in Scripture's phrasing, therefore election is from foresight of faith. Rather: therefore to all the elect in their time saving faith is given. If the argument had force I could invert it: Believers, when salvation is in view, always means the elect; therefore no saving faith except of the elect; therefore faith arises from antecedent election. From such word-use you may conclude only that faith and election have a nexus — not whether foresight of faith precedes election as a prerequired condition (as Remonstrants will), or faith follows election as a disposition to be produced in all the elect at the due time. The cited places do not settle that; weighing them one by one is needless.
